responses: After thoughtful discussion with fellow committee members, I’ve come to support a balanced but prioritized allocation that reflects both immediate needs and long-term community well-being. I believe the $10 million should be distributed as follows: 30% to EDUCATION, 25% to INFRASTRUCTURE, 20% to HEALTHCARE, 15% to GREEN SPACES, and 10% to ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT. I was initially inclined to prioritize education more heavily, especially given the data on declining test scores and teacher turnover, but I was persuaded by colleagues that reliable infrastructure—particularly broadband and public transit—is foundational for both education (remote learning, teacher recruitment) and economic opportunity. Healthcare and green spaces are also critical for quality of life, and while economic development is important, I believe it will be most effective when supported by strong schools, health, and infrastructure. This allocation aims to create a resilient, equitable, and thriving community for all residents.

I would recommend allocating 30% to EDUCATION, 20% to HEALTHCARE, 20% to INFRASTRUCTURE, 15% to GREEN SPACES, and 15% to ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT. Education is foundational—our declining test scores and high teacher turnover signal a crisis that could lead to long-term population loss, especially as families consider moving for better schools. Investing heavily here not only improves immediate outcomes but also supports future workforce readiness and community stability. Healthcare and infrastructure are critical for quality of life and economic resilience, while green spaces and economic development foster community well-being and local opportunity. This balanced approach prioritizes education as the anchor, while ensuring no essential area is neglected.

I believe we should prioritize education with about 30% of the $10 million grant, because strong schools are foundational to our community’s long-term success. The data shows student performance is declining and teacher turnover is high, which not only affects learning but also makes families consider leaving Greenfield. Investing in teacher recruitment, after-school programs, and scholarships can help reverse these trends and make our schools a draw, not a reason to leave. While healthcare, green spaces, infrastructure, and economic development are all important, I see education as the anchor—when kids are well-supported, they’re more likely to stay in town, contribute to the economy, and build a healthier, more vibrant community for everyone.

Ultimately, I’m confident this allocation will create a sustainable, inclusive foundation for Greenfield’s future.

I’d recommend allocating 30% to healthcare, 25% to green spaces, 20% to education, 15% to infrastructure, and 10% to economic development—balancing urgent needs with long-term growth.
